items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4186

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public service law, in relation to directing the
public service commission study the feasibility and the costs of burying
all or most of the electrical, telephone and internet transmission lines
in New York state and to publish and deliver a report of its findings to
the governor and the legislature, and requiring new electrical, tele-
phone and internet transmission lines to be buried underground

 
PURPOSE:

To require the Public Service Commission to study and report on the
feasibility and the costs of burying all or most of the electrical,
telephone and internet transmission lines in New York State, and to
require new electrical, telephone and internet transmission lines to be
buried underground.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 creates two new sections to the Public Service Law: 119-d and
119-e.  New section 119-d (1) provides that the Public Service Commis-
sion

(PSC) shall conduct a study to analyze the feasibility and the costs of
burying underground all or most of the existing electrical, telephone
and internet transmission lines in New York State.  Such report shall
include an analysis of:

(a) the economic and environmental benefits from burying such existing
lines; and

(b) the economic cost burden of doing so, including an estimate of what
the cost per utility customer would be, the number jobs to be created to
complete the project and a timeline for completion of the project

2. In analyzing the costs and benefits for purposes of this study, the
PSC shall consider the varying geographical areas of the State and
report separately on the impact particular areas might have on the
project. The study shall also quantify the economic costs and benefits
of burying existing electrical, telephone and internet transmission
lines to utility customers and shall separate the results by utility.
The study shall calculate the cost per customer of the entire cost of
project statewide, redardless of where the customer lives, for.the life
of the project on a monthly basis.

The report shall be published within 140 days of the act becoming law
and the PSC shall (a) publish the report on its website and (b) deliver
or copy of the report to the governor, the temporary president of the
senate, the Speaker of the Assembly and the chair of the senate eneregy
and telecommunication committee and the chair of assembly energy commit-
tee New Section 119-e mandates that all new electrical, telephone and
inter-net transmission lines installed in the State shall be buried
underground.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Every time there is a forecast of a major storm; New Yorkers live in
fear that they will have to suffer another power outage. How many times
do we have to live through this nightmare with wind and rainstorms in
the summer and fall and blizzards in the winter? It took the Great Bliz-
zard of 1888, for New York City to bury its power and telephone poles.
We should not have to wait any longer.  The tropical storm Isaias was a
brief, but it did its damage quickly.  Just in my Assembly District
alone, over 57% of customers in the City of Newburgh, 35t in the Town of
Newburgh, 26% in the City of Poughkeepsie and 24% in the City of Beacon
were affected and lost power. It has taken two to three days on average
to restore power throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley Region.

The cost of burying transmission lines pales to the inconvenience and
costs to individuals and businesses every time there is a major storm.
Workers lose time from work as businesses are forced to close due to
loss of electricity and internet connection. People must throw out
spoiled food.

The cost of burying the lines will be passed on to the consumer over a
number of years. This is a small price to pay for the peace ot mind that
you won't lose power and your internet connection. Such a project will
take years, but it will create thousands of jobs.  Burying transmission
lines will encourage the transmission of hydroelectric power and wind
power without unsightly transmission lines which currently foster oppo-
sition.

The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over and
expecting a different result. This recurring problem will go away by
itself. We must explore new options.

None. New bill.

This act shall take effect immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4186A

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act directing the public service commission to study the feasibility
and the costs of burying all or most of the electrical, telephone and
internet transmission lines in New York state and to publish and deliver
a report of its findings to the governor and the legislature, and
requiring new electrical, telephone and internet transmission lines to
be buried underground

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would require the Public Service Commission to study and
report on the feasibility and the costs of burying all or most of the
electrical, telephone, and internet transmission lines in New York
State. The Public Service Commission would publish and deliver a report
of its findings to the Governor and Legislature.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires the Public Service Commission to conduct a study to
analyze the feasibility and the costs of burying underground all or most
of the existing electrical, telephone, and internet transmission lines
in New York, including an analysis of the economic and environmental
benefits from burying such existing lines the economic cost burden of
doing so, and a timeline for completion of the overall project. Such
study shall be completed within one year following the effective date of
this Act.

Section 2 is the effective date.

 
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ORIGINAL AND AMENDED VERSION (IF APPLICABLE):

The amended version retains only the study portion of the bill. It elim-
inates the section mandating that all future electrical, telephone and
internet transmission lines installed in the State be buried.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Every time a major storm is forecast, New Yorkers live in fear that they
will suffer yet another power outage. How many times do we have to live
through a recurring nightmare caused by wind and rainstorms in the
summer and fall and blizzards in the winter? It took the Great Blizzard
of 1888 to have New York City begin to bury most of its power and tele-
phone lines. It's long past time for the rest of the state to follow
suit.

Tropical Storm Isaias was brief, but it caused outsize damage to trans-
mission lines. In my Assembly District alone, more than 57% of customers
in the City of Newburgh, 35% in the Town of Newburgh, 26% in the City of
Poughkeepsie, and 24% in the City of Beacon were affected and lost
power. It took two to three days on average to restore power throughout
the Mid-Hudson Valley Region.

The cost of burying transmission lines pales in comparison to the incon-
venience and costs to individuals and businesses every time there is a
major storm. According to data from the New York State Public Service
Commission, between January 1, 2012 and July 26, 2020, New York utili-
ties spent well over $2 billion to restore interrupted electric, gas,
and communication services after major storms. Workers lose time from
work as businesses are forced to close due to loss of electricity and
internet connection. People must throw out spoiled food.

The breakdown of the costs of storms to electric and gas companies from
January I, 2012 to July 26, 2020 is as follows:

Central Hudson $56,644,699

Con Edison - $361,859,851

Niagara Mohawk - $230,813,487

New York State Electric and Gas - $425,121,532

Orange and Rockland - $133,422,875

Rochester Gas and Electric - $92,437,314

PSEG Long Island - $587,746,807

The cost of burying the lines will be passed on to the consumer over a
number of years. This is a small price to pay for peace of mind and
uninterrupted power and internet service. Such a project will take
years, but it will create thousands of jobs. Burying transmission lines
will also encourage the transmission of hydroelectric power and wind
power without necessitating the unsightly transmission lines which
currently foster opposition.

The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over and
expecting a different result. This recurring problem will not go away by
itself. We must explore new options.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2019-20: A10900-A - Amend and recommit to Corporations, Authorities and
Commissions S8931-A - Amend and recommit to Rules

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
